lead: Tallahassee is inland and hilly, but storms still hit hard. Hurricanes, tornadoes and its famous tree canopy mean many water damage calls start with a fallen limb.
risk: storm and tree damage, roof leaks and heavy rain
why: Tallahassee is proud of its live oaks and canopy roads, but those trees can come down in a storm. In 2016, Hurricane Hermine knocked out power to most of the city, the first hurricane to hit Florida in more than a decade. Two years later, Hurricane Michael brought more fallen trees and outages. On May 10, 2024, several tornadoes tore through town and damaged hundreds of homes.

A tree on the roof lets in rain fast, and ceilings and walls can soak through before a tarp goes up. Heavy summer storms also flood low streets near Lake Munson and the Lafayette Park area. Only about 40% of homes are owner-occupied, since Florida State and FAMU bring in many renters. Leaks in rentals often take longer to report, so damage spreads.
image_alt: Two workers installing new roof decking
image_caption: After a tree hits the roof, damaged decking is replaced before a Tallahassee home is dried out.
problems: Canopy streets in Betton Hills, Myers Park
Low areas in Lafayette Park, near Lake Munson
tips: Have large oaks near the house checked by an arborist.
Keep a roof tarp and plastic sheeting ready before storm season.
Clear gutters of oak leaves in fall and spring.
Renters: report leaks in writing and take photos right away.
areas: Calls come from Midtown, Frenchtown, All Saints, Killearn, Myers Park, Betton Hills, Southwood and Lafayette Park, plus Crawfordville, Quincy and Havana.

faq.q: What should I do if a tree falls on my Tallahassee roof?
faq.a: Get everyone out of the rooms below and stay clear of downed wires. Call your insurer and a tree service. Once it is safe, the roof needs a tarp to stop more rain. DryFlare can dry the ceilings, walls and floors so mold does not take hold.
